question: Explain the diffraction pattern produced by a single narrow slit. Why is the central maximum broader and brighter than the secondary maxima? Support your answer using the conditions for minima.

options.A: Single-slit diffraction gives equal-width bright maxima of equal intensity. Minima occur at $a\sin\theta=(n+\tfrac12)\lambda$, and the central maximum is narrowest.
options.B: The central maximum is bright only because the slit is brightest at its centre; diffraction and path difference have no role.
options.C: Minima occur at $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$, but the central maximum has angular width $\dfrac{\lambda}{a}$ and is weaker than the secondary maxima.
options.D: Each point of a narrow slit acts as a secondary source, so their superposition gives a broad central maximum and weaker secondary maxima. Minima occur at $a\sin\theta=n\lambda$ ($n=1,2,\ldots$). The central maximum lies between the first minima on both sides, hence its angular width is $\dfrac{2\lambda}{a}$ for small angles. At the centre, all wavelets have zero path difference and arrive in phase, so it is brightest; off-centre, only partial constructive interference occurs, so secondary maxima are weaker.
